notes.meaning: God spoke to Joshua right after all the people safely reached the other side. This event brought their forty years of wandering in the desert to an end and led them into the promised land. God guided his people step by step, giving new instructions only as each part of the crossing was completed.

differ.view: Crossing the Jordan into Canaan pictures entering entire sanctification, where a believer's heart is cleansed from inward sin and wholly given over to God.
Crossing the river pictures a believer entering spiritual victory and rest in Christ by faith, or passing through death into the promised land of heaven.

notes.meaning: God told Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Even the tribes who chose to live on the east side of the river had a representative. This showed that all the tribes remained united as one family under God.

Each man was ordered to lift a heavy stone from the riverbed where the priests were standing. They were to carry these stones across the river to their campsite for the night. Taking stones from the deepest part of the river proved that God had truly made the bed dry.

Joshua called the twelve chosen men and sent them near the ark of the covenant in the riverbed. Each man picked up a large stone and placed it on his shoulder, one for every tribe. Carrying these heavy stones took real effort and let each tribe share in honoring God's miracle.

The stones were meant to catch the attention of children in years to come. When children asked what the heap meant, parents were to tell how the Lord cut off the waters of the Jordan before the ark. The monument stood as a permanent sign to help Israel remember God's power and kindness.

The twelve men obeyed Joshua's command and carried the river stones to their campsite. Because they represented the tribes, their action was counted as the work of the whole nation. God gave them these stones from the riverbed as a visible token that the land was now their own.

Joshua also set up a second monument of twelve stones right in the riverbed where the priests had stood. These stones marked the exact place of God's presence during the crossing and could likely be seen when the water was low. They remained as an enduring witness for years afterward to remind everyone of the miracle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this verse as a duplicate record added from a separate source, or suggest reading the Hebrew to mean stones were taken out of the river rather than placed inside it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writers such as Augustine interpreted the two sets of twelve stones as symbols of the twelve patriarchs and twelve apostles, and linked the river crossing to baptism.

notes.meaning: The priests stood completely still with the ark in the river channel until the entire crossing was finished. Meanwhile, the people hurried across the dry riverbed, perhaps from a mix of eagerness and fear of the suspended water. Both the priests' quiet patience and the people's swift steps showed deep respect for God's presence.

Once all the people had safely reached the western bank, the priests carried the ark across before everyone's eyes. The ark crossed last because the Lord's presence was what held back the water the entire time. The people watched in awe as the sacred chest led them into their new home.

About forty thousand armed men from Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh marched at the front of the army. They had already received their land east of the Jordan, but they kept their promise to help the other tribes conquer Canaan. Their presence gave great courage to the rest of the nation as they entered enemy territory.

The Lord lifted up Joshua's standing before all the people on that very day. The Israelites saw that God was guiding him, and they respected his leadership just as they had respected Moses. God gave him this honor so the nation would follow him faithfully into battle.

The priests remained in the river channel until God gave the command through Joshua. Joshua told them to come up, and they obeyed at once. This showed that both Joshua and the priests moved only when the Lord directed them.

As soon as the priests stepped out of the river channel onto dry land, the waters rushed back. The Jordan quickly overflowed its banks just as it had before the crossing. This proved beyond doubt that the river had stopped because of God's power, not by accident.

Israel crossed the river on the tenth day of the first month and set up camp at Gilgal, near Jericho. This was the exact day when families chose lambs to prepare for Passover, just five days short of forty years after leaving Egypt. God timed their arrival so their entrance into the land would match a holy feast of remembrance.

Joshua arranged the twelve stones brought from the riverbed into a memorial at Gilgal. They were likely stacked or placed in a row so anyone passing by could easily count them. This marker served as an enduring sign of their first campsite in the land God had promised.

Joshua told the people that their children would one day ask what these stones meant. Parents were responsible to teach their children how God brought Israel across the Jordan on dry land. Sharing these true stories kept faith alive from one generation to the next.

Joshua compared the drying up of the Jordan to the parting of the Red Sea forty years earlier. Even though many in the camp were not born yet when the sea parted, they shared in that mercy as members of the same covenant family. Remembering older wonders helps believers trust that God never changes.

God performed this miracle so all the surrounding nations would learn that his hand is mighty. It was also meant to teach Israel to honor and revere the Lord throughout every generation. Remembering God's greatness leads his people to trust and obey him in everyday life.
